subtype: Approach: keeping it because nobody saw [Pitfall]
passage: The hundred-rupee note lay by the paan stall, curled like a leaf. Bhupen looked left, looked right, and pocketed it. Nobody saw. All morning at school it sat there like a warm stone. At recess Amandeep offered to share chips and Bhupen said no, he was not hungry, though he was. In maths the sums swam. Each time a teacher glanced his way his ears went hot, though nobody asked him anything. That evening he walked back past the paan stall and stared at the empty spot on the pavement. He still had the note in his pocket that night, and no wish to spend it.

qa.q: How much money did Bhupen pick up?
qa.a: He picked up a hundred-rupee note.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling in class?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty, since his ears went hot every time a teacher glanced his way.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do to ease this feeling, and why?
qa.a: He could give the note to the stall owner or a teacher in case the owner returns, which would end the worry that follows him.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have wondered when Bhupen refused the chips?
qa.a: Amandeep may have wondered why Bhupen said he was not hungry, since something seemed to be wrong.

grounding: A boy pockets money because no one saw, and spends the day uneasy, caught by his own guilt rather than by anyone.

passage:
"Santosh, why are you so quiet today?"
"Nothing, Tenzin."
"You haven't said one joke, bhai. You didn't even eat your samosa."
"I'm not hungry."
"Is it the hundred-rupee note? The one you picked up this morning?"
"...Nobody saw."
"I saw."
"You're not nobody. Nobody else saw."
"So why do you keep touching your pocket?"
"I don't know. It feels hot."
"You've been weird all day."
"Because I keep thinking someone's looking for it. That old man at the bus stop kept checking his pockets."
"So give it back."
"What if he thinks I stole it?"

qa.q: How was Santosh feeling all day?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy, as if the note in his pocket was hot, and couldn't stop thinking about the owner.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Santosh, and why?
qa.a: He could go with Tenzin to a teacher or the bus stop shopkeeper and explain, because an adult can help return it without blame.

qa.q: How does Santosh's mood look to Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin notices he isn't himself and guesses the reason, worried for a friend and wanting him to fix it.

grounding: It shows a boy pocketing a hundred-rupee note because nobody saw, then spending the day uneasy, caught more by guilt than by anyone's eyes.

passage: Last month I found a hundred-rupee note lying on the road near our colony gate. Nobody was around. I put it in my pocket and thought, lucky day. At school, I told myself I'd buy chips and a comic. But the whole day felt wrong. Every time the teacher looked at me, I felt she knew. I kept touching my pocket. At lunch my friend Naveen asked why I wasn't eating. I didn't buy anything. On the way home I kept looking at the road, as if someone would still be searching. Nobody had seen me, but I felt watched all day. That night I told Amma, and she said, "Hemant, let's give it to the watchman at the gate. People ask him first."

qa.q: Where did Hemant find the note?
qa.a: On the road near the colony gate.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel through the school day?
qa.a: Hemant felt uneasy and guilty, as if watched, even though nobody had seen.

qa.q: What else could Hemant have done that morning, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could have given it to the watchman at the gate straight away, because that is where people come back to ask.

qa.q: How does the note look to Amma?
qa.a: Amma sees it calmly, not as a crime, and gives Hemant a simple way to return it.

grounding: It shows a child pocketing a found note because no one saw, then being troubled all day by guilt more than by anyone's eyes.
